title: PO12Q - Quantitative Political Analysis: Uncovering Relationships
text:
Welcome!

If you are resitting the module, then please click on “Archives” in the top right-hand corner and select “2025-2026 Academic Year”. The main page is being updated for the academic year 2026/27.

Welcome to “Quantitative Political Analytics: Uncovering Relationships”. This module extends PO11Q into bivariate and multivariate analysis, equipping you with the tools to answer real-world research questions with statistical rigour. We start with what is arguably the hardest question in empirical political science: what does it take to say because? Causality is fundamentally a matter of research design – no statistical method can conjure it from observational data alone. But understanding what causal inference demands helps you interpret your results honestly and avoid overclaiming.
With this standard in mind, we turn to two complementary methods. Correlation analysis detects whether a pattern exists between variables. Linear regression goes beyond that pattern: it tells you not just that a relationship exists, but how large it is, in what direction, and how confidently you can speak about it. Because regression is the workhorse of quantitative political science, we examine it in depth: how well a model fits the data, how multiple independent variables can be combined to explain a single outcome, and what assumptions must hold for the results to be meaningful.
This is the online companion to the seminars on PO12Q. The companion is structured very much in the same way as last term. But it introduces a new feature, called the “Weekly Code-Along”. Here, I walk you through an applied example in a short video to illustrate the method or technique we are covering in that respective week in R. Work through these sections either before you come to the seminar to get a bit of a head start, or after to consolidate the knowledge you have gained in the seminar.
In addition, you will find the following supplementary materials embedded throughout the companion:

Videos that illustrate specific methods or techniques
Applications that explore specific techniques in more detail
Flashcards (with csv files) to learn the R functions used each week

To make working with the module’s material a little easier, I have produced the following resources which are available in the Downloads Section:

A collection of Statistical Tables we will use
A Formula Collection which contains all the formulae used on the module (you will receive an identical one in the exam, so there is no need to memorise anything)
A complete bibliography of sources used for the module

I hope you find it useful!

 



Companion Features
You will find embedded in the text five different types of boxes which serve different purposes:

Some explanations that will hopefully make your work with this webpage or learning the material itself easier.


A brief question which tests your understanding of the previous material.


To help you a bit along the way through the module, I have recorded a few videos.


This appears when you need to be careful with your coding in R to avoid problems.


This box appears whenever I want you to stop at a particular point in the worksheet and to flag up to me that you are done.



Accessibility
The companion uses the font “Lexend”. Lexend fonts are intended to reduce visual stress and so improve reading performance. Initially they were designed with dyslexia and struggling readers in mind, but Bonnie Shaver-Troup, creator of the Lexend project, soon found out that these fonts are also great for everyone else.
Code is displayed in Recursive Mono. The font’s characters share the same width for clear legibility and perfect alignment. This is particularly helpful for use in programming and data-heavy design tasks, but also allows for creative possibilities in display typography.
Equations and mathematical expressions are set in Fira Math. Fira Math is easy to read with open shapes, clear spacing, and good contrast. This keeps subscripts, superscripts, and fractions legible - even at small sizes. It stays readable on screens and in print, reducing mix-ups between look-alike characters like 1, I, and l.
If the three-column layout feels too busy, click the small text icon in the companion’s top-right to switch to Reader Mode. This streamlines the page and minimises the table of contents into a compact bar at the top.
All figures include descriptive alt text, and all embedded videos, interactive applications, and flashcard panels carry descriptive labels. Users relying on a screen reader will therefore receive a meaningful description of every visual element rather than a generic filename or placeholder.
The companion also uses a dark mode theme. For many users, including some neurodivergent individuals, dark mode can reduce eye strain and enhance focus by minimising visual overstimulation.
Whilst I recognise that mobile phones play an essential part in all our daily lives, please note that this companion is optimised for display on tablets, laptops, and desktop computers.

title: Week 3
text:
Motivation1
The word “matrix” generally conjures up levels of horror in students which even Stephen King would be struggling to match2. And I have to admit that I have not always been best friends with them myself, either. But they are useful, and in their ability to convey a large amount of information in a structured and logical way, they are even beautiful. Because at the end of the day, a matrix is nothing more than a list.
In the lecture I introduced you to the following equation to describe an observation in a population:
\[\begin{equation}
y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x_{i} + \epsilon_{i}
\end{equation}\]
If we wanted to write out this equation for every observation in our data set, it would look something like this:
\[\begin{align*}
    y_{1} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x_{1} + \epsilon_{1} \\
    y_{2} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x_{2} + \epsilon_{2} \\
    &\vdots \\
    y_{n} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x_{n} + \epsilon_{n}
\end{align*}\]
This is incredibly wasteful, as it unnecessarily repeats notation. What we could do instead is to create a list which has as many columns as there are unique elements in these equations (since they all have the same structure), and only note the numeric values which actually change. And there you have a matrix:




\(\pmb{y}\)


\(=\)


\(\pmb{X}\)


\(\pmb{\beta}\)


\(+\)


\(\pmb{\epsilon}\)






\(\downarrow\)




\(\downarrow\)


\(\downarrow\)




\(\downarrow\)






\(\begin{bmatrix}
      y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n
      \end{bmatrix}\)


=


\(\begin{bmatrix}
      1 & x_1 \\
      1 & x_2 \\
      \vdots & \vdots \\
      1 & x_n
      \end{bmatrix}\)


\(\begin{bmatrix}
      \beta_0 \\
      \beta_1
      \end{bmatrix}\)


+


\(\begin{bmatrix}
      \epsilon_1 \\
      \epsilon_2 \\
      \vdots \\
      \epsilon_n
      \end{bmatrix}\)



You may have noticed that I have set the elements which refer to a matrix in bold. This is deliberate. Going forward we will distinguish between the following three types of elements:

Scalar

A single numerical value, typically representing:

a constant (like \(3\), \(\pi\), or \(0.05\)),
a parameter (like \(\beta_0\)),
or an individual data point (like \(x_{i,j}\) or \(y_i\)).




Vector
A vector is a list of values arranged in a specific order. Most often, we write vectors as columns - meaning they have one value per row.
Key properties:

A vector is one column and multiple rows (a “column vector”).
It holds multiple values, but is still considered one object.
We use bold lowercase letters to name vectors: \(\pmb{x}\), \(\pmb{y}\), \(\pmb{\hat{\epsilon}}\).

Example:
A column vector of residuals \(\pmb{\hat{\epsilon}}\):
\[
\pmb{\hat{\epsilon}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat{\epsilon}_1 \\
\hat{\epsilon}_2 \\
\vdots \\
\hat{\epsilon}_n
\end{bmatrix}
\]


Matrix
A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers with rows and columns. It’s a way to organize data, equations, or systems neatly.
Key properties:

A matrix has multiple rows and multiple columns.
We write matrices in square brackets.
The size of a matrix is written as “rows × columns” (e.g., a 3 × 2 matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns).
We use bold uppercase letters to name matrices: \(\pmb{X}\), \(\pmb{A}\).

Example:
A \(3 \times 2\) matrix \(\pmb{X}\):
\[
\pmb{X} =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} \\
x_{21} & x_{22} \\
x_{31} & x_{32}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Whilst we will be using all three in weeks to come, let us now focus on matrices. To show you how to work with matrices, let us define two matrices:
\[\begin{equation*}
    \pmb{A}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
        1 & 7 & 3\\
        9 & 5 & 4\\
    \end{bmatrix}
    \hspace{0.75cm}
    \pmb{B}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    6 & 3 & 8 & 2 \\
    3 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\
    1 & 5 & 3 & 9 \\
    \end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}\]

Matrix Notation
We can refer to individual elements of a matrix by stating the name of the matrix, and then in the index first the row, followed by the column (you might recognise this logic from R – this is because it is the same). With respect to matrix \(\pmb{A}\), for example, the value in the first row and first column (1) would be referred to as:
\(\pmb{A}_{11} = 1\)
The number in the first row, but second column would be referred to as:
\(\pmb{A}_{12} = 7\)

What is the value of \(\pmb{B}_{23}\)?

title: Week 3
text:
Calculating with Matrices
We will only need to multiply and divide matrices on this module, so let’s cover these operations now.

Multiplying Matrices
To show you how this is done, I will multiply matrix \(\pmb{A}\) with matrix \(\pmb{B}\) and record the results in a new matrix called \(\pmb{C}\).
\[\begin{equation*}
    \pmb{A} \times \pmb{B} = \pmb{C}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 7 & 3\\
    9 & 5 & 4\\
    \end{bmatrix}
    \times
    \begin{bmatrix}
    6 & 3 & 8 & 2 \\
    3 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\
    1 & 5 & 3 & 9 \\
    \end{bmatrix}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    30 & 32 & 24 &  51\\
    73 & 57 &  89 &  74\\
    \end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}\]
In order to calculate a new element \(\pmb{C}_{i,j}\), we multiply the elements of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) row of \(\pmb{A}\) with the elements of the \(j^{\text{th}}\) column of \(\pmb{B}\). We then add together these so-called inner products in order to arrive at \(\pmb{C}_{i,j}\). Let me give you some examples in which I have set the values from matrix \(\pmb{A}\) in bold to make the process more transparent.
\(\pmb{C}_{11} = \textbf{1}\times6 + \textbf{7}\times3 + \textbf{3}\times1 = 30\)
\(\pmb{C}_{12} = \textbf{1}\times3 + \textbf{7}\times2 + \textbf{3}\times5 = 32\)
\(\pmb{C}_{21} = \textbf{9}\times6 + \textbf{5}\times3 + \textbf{4}\times1 = 73\)
I have prepared a short video taking you through this process step by step. I would encourage you to watch it now.

If you can’t get enough of my delightful German accent, then I have some videos for you in which I go through the respective operation with matrices on screen. Here is the first:
Multiplying Matrices




Assume we are multiplying a 4x3 matrix with a 3x4 matrix with one another. How many rows and columns does the resulting matrix have?



Dividing Matrices
In order to be able to divide by an entire matrix, we take its inverse, and then multiply with the inverse3. We do the same in the non-matrix world. For example, if we wanted to divide 6 by 3, this is the same as multiplying 6 with \(\frac{1}{3}\), the inverse of 3. Sadly, inverting a matrix is not quite as straightforward as this. In fact, it is one of the most challenging operations you can do with a matrix. Luckily, the inversion of a 2 by 2 matrix (which is what we will be using) is still possible without a degree in algebra. The inverse \(D^{-1}\) of a 2 by 2 matrix \(D\) is defined as
\[\begin{equation*}
    \pmb{D}^{-1} =
    \begin{bmatrix}
        a & b \\
        c & d \\
    \end{bmatrix}^{-1}
    =
    \frac{1}{ad - bc}
    \begin{bmatrix}
        d & -b \\
        -c & a \\
    \end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}\]
Thus, to arrive at the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix, we first have to form the fraction in front of it. This takes as its denominator the difference between the products of the diagonal elements. We also refer to the denominator as the determinant of the matrix. In a second step – now in the matrix itself – we swap a and d, and set a minus sign in front of b and c.

title: Week 7
text:
Exporting the Results
As for the graphs, you can also export and save the results of the regression model in a Word table. To do that you can use the ‘modelsummary’ package.
Just like writing a shopping list, we start by creating a list of models for which we want modelsummary to produce a table. You can merely list the names of the objects in which the models are stored, or you can give them specific names which will appear as column titles in the table. This addition is by no means a must, but sometimes you might wish to give models a particular name, for example if you have used different methods of estimation, different components of a theory, etc. In the table we are creating here, I wish to distinguish between bivariate and multivariate models. By default, modelsummary just numbers models in ascending order.

models <- list(
  "Bivariate"    = model
)

This simple step is already sufficient to produce – an admittedly somewhat crude – results table. All we have to do is to load the modelsummary package and to use the previously defined list of models as the argument of the modelsummary() function:

library(modelsummary)
modelsummary(models)


Execute these code chunks as we go through this Section, so you can see the alterations we make to the table in real-time.

This table is a vast improvement on the raw R output you would receive when calling summary(model1). But it is far from finished. One characteristic which is conspicuously absent is an assessment of statistical significance. In model summaries of this kind this information is usually provided in the form of asterisks or other symbols next to the respective coefficient. We can add these simply by adding the option stars=TRUE to the code.

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE)

Next up is the modification of the stub. The stub is the leftmost column in which you name the indicators for which coefficients will be presented.In the stub, “[a]bbreviate nothing. And never ever ever use computer variable names to stand for concepts. These are personal code words that convey no meaning to readers.” (Stimson, n.d., p. 10) Following this advice, let us add proper labels to the independent variables.
To let modelsummary know how to replace each variable name, we create a so-called coefficient map. This is really just a character vector which follows a “before-after” logic in each of its rows. For example 'age'='Age' replaces the variable name age with the label Age. We need to do this for all the variables we used in our models. I am storing this in a vecor called cm which stands for coefficient map.

cm <- c('ALCOHOL'    = 'Hospital stays related to alcohol use',
        '(Intercept)' = 'Intercept')

The next step is easy, as we only need to feed this coefficient map into the modelsummary code with the option coef_map=cm:

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm)

This is a personal thing, but I also like to show the label of the dependent variable in results tables. They just feel incomplete to me without this information. There is no default to achieve this in modelsummary and so we need to use a little trick.
What I want to add in the first row, but only in the second columm, the text . This requires us to alter the style of the table slightly. modelsummary uses another package called tinytable to style the output. We load the package with library(tinytable) and instruct R to place the text where we want it.

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm)|>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable: GCSE Score" = 2))

Lastly, let us tackle the model fit statistics. By default, modelsummary prints a whole festival of these into the bottom section of the table, but I want to concentrate only on R\(^2\).

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm,
             gof_omit = 'DF|Deviance|Log.Lik|F|AIC|BIC|RMSE|Adj')|>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable: GCSE Score" = 2))

You can export your tables for use in MS Word, or Apple Pages. The easiest way to do this, is to add save_tt() at the end of your code, and to specify the file name you wish to save it as. The resulting png will be placed in your working directory, so you can copy and paste it into your document.

section: Working with the Classical Linear Assumptions
text:
Working with the Classical Linear Assumptions
To help you understand the assumptions, I have written an application which illustrates how violations of key OLS regression assumptions affect estimation and inference.

  Open Application      

You start by simulating a base dataset. In a second step, you apply one of these three common assumption violations:

Nonlinearity: the true relationship includes a quadratic term, but the fitted model is linear.

Heteroscedasticity: the error variance increases with \(x\), so residuals spread out unevenly.

Collinearity: predictors \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are highly correlated, making coefficient estimates unstable.


How to use the app

Choose the sample size and the true coefficients (\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\)) in the left panel.

Click Simulate data to generate the base dataset.

Select a violation scenario and adjust its sliders to control severity.

The main plot shows the data, fitted line(s), and diagnostic curves.

The Diagnostics box reports statistical checks such as Breusch–Pagan, RESET, or VIF, depending on the scenario.

The Model comparison box contrasts the fitted equation with and without the violation.

You can reset everything with the Reset button and repeat with different settings to see how results vary.


Exercises with the app

Sampling variability and the true parameter: Click Simulate data several times with the default settings (\(\beta_1 = 1\)).

Record \(\hat\beta_1\) from three different simulations. Are they identical? Why not?
Now increase \(n\) to 1000 and repeat. What happens to the spread of your estimates across simulations?

What heteroscedasticity does – and doesn’t – break: Switch to Heteroscedasticity. Start with the slider at 0, then increase it gradually.

Does \(\hat\beta_1\) itself shift systematically as you increase the slider, or does it stay near the true value? What does this tell you about bias under heteroscedasticity?
Compare SE (OLS) and SE (HC3) in the diagnostics table. Which standard error should you trust when the Breusch-Pagan test rejects, and why?

The cost of ignoring nonlinearity: Switch to Nonlinearity. Set \(\beta_2 = 0\) first (confirm it matches your base sample), then increase \(\beta_2\) to around 0.5 or higher.

Look at the orange linear fit and the dashed quadratic. Where does the linear model systematically over- or under-predict \(y\)?
Check the Linear vs quadratic (F-test) p-value. At what point does it reject? What real-world consequence would fitting a straight line to curved data have for your predictions?

Why collinearity makes you uncertain, not wrong: Switch to Collinearity. Set \(\rho = 0.5\), note the estimates, then increase \(\rho\) toward 0.99.

Watch VIF and the standard errors in the coefficient table. What happens as \(\rho\) rises?
In Model output, compare \(\hat\beta_1\) estimated with both regressors versus with \(x_1\) only. Why do they differ, and which one has a causal interpretation if \(x_2\) is a genuine confounder?
Run the simulation a few times at high \(\rho\). Do the individual estimates jump around a lot between draws?



The Gauss-Markov Theorem and Making your Regression BLUE

An estimator (such as \(\hat{\beta}_{1}\)) is considered the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) of \(\beta_{1}\) if the following conditions are met:

\(\hat{\beta}_{1}\) is a linear function of a random variable, such as the dependent variable \(Y\) in the regression model.
\(\hat{\beta}_{1}\) is unbiased, that is, its average or expected value, \(E(\hat{\beta}_{1})\), is equal to the true value, \(\beta_{1}\)
\(\hat{\beta}_{1}\) has minimum variance in the class of all such linear unbiased estimators; an unbiased estimator with the least variance is known as an efficient estimator.


For estimators to be BLUE, the following of the Classical Linear Assumptions (CLA) need to hold:

Functional form (linearity in parameters)
Zero conditional mean error terms
Homoscedasticity
No autocorrelation
No perfect multicollinearity (and \(n > k\))

Testing the Classical Linear Assumptions in R
For this worksheet we will be using the london data set from the lectures, this time with the following variables:
 





Table 1: Codebook for london_11 Data Set











Variable
Label
Year

2017/18









 
Data are taken from GOV.UK (2013), London Data Store (2010), and House of Commons Library (n.d.).

Homoscedasticity

Load the data set london_11.csv as an object called london
Subset the data to a random sample as follows:

set.seed(123)
london_sam <- sample_frac(london, 0.65, replace=FALSE)

Regress GCSE scores on income and interpret the results.

model1 <- lm(gcse ~ income, data=london_sam)

Breusch-Pagan Test by Hand

Extract the residuals from model 1 and store their squared values in a new object called ressq.

ressq <- resid(model1)^2

Regress the squared residuals on the original independent variable.

model1res <- lm(ressq~income, data=london_sam)

Store the number of observations of this new model in an object called N.

N <- nobs(model1res)

Obtain the model fit measure R\(^2\) for this model.
Calculate the test-statistic for the Breusch-Pagan test as the product of N and R\(^2\).

chisq <- 0.001857*N

Conduct a Chi-Squared test with one degree of freedom.

pchisq(chisq, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE)

[1] 0.7676653



Breusch-Pagan Test with the lmtest package.

Install and load the lmtest package
Conduct a Breusch-Pagan Test with the lmtest package.

bptest(model1)

Compare the results with the results obtained in Exercise 4f.

Heteroscedasticity

Now let’s introduce heteroscedasticity:

london_heterosc <- filter(london, income<28000 | income>100000)


Why does this code lead to heteroscedasticity?

Estimate a new model, and note the significance of coefficients.

model2 <- lm(gcse ~ income, data=london_heterosc)

As before, conduct a Breusch-Pagan Test with the lmtest package.

bptest(model2)

Install and load the sandwich package.

library(sandwich)

The sandwich package corrects standard errors for heteroscedasticity by replacing the single \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) with observation-level weights. The default is HC3 – if you ever work with somebody using Stata then you need to replace this with HC1 to obtain the same results.
First, display the diagonal of the classical variance-covariance matrix, which assumes homoscedasticity (i.e. \(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}\)). These diagonal entries are the variances of each coefficient estimate — their square roots give you the standard errors you see in summary():

diag(vcov(model2))

 (Intercept)       income 
2.140830e+00 1.559712e-10 


Due to heteroscedasticity, these variances are likely incorrect, however. Let us re-estimate them with the sandwich package which corrects for heteroscedasticity:

diag(vcovHC(model2, type="HC3"))

 (Intercept)       income 
1.066967e+01 4.883682e-10 


These are obviously different. But what does the HC3 correction actually do? Recall that the variance-covariance matrix of our coefficients is \(\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \hat{\sigma}^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\). When we called diag(vcov(model2)) above, R calculated the diagonal elements of precisely this matrix.
The HC3 correction in diag(vcovHC(model2, type="HC3")) targets \(\hat{\sigma}^2\): the Classical Linear Assumptions assume that every observation has the same error variance \(\sigma^2\), which we estimate with \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). In matrix form, the estimated error variance-covariance matrix is:
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2 \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix}
\hat{\sigma}^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \hat{\sigma}^2 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \hat{\sigma}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The HC3 correction drops that assumption: instead of using a single \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) on the diagonal, it calculates an individual weight for each observation. Observations that the model fits poorly (i.e. have a larger residual) get a larger weight, allowing them to contribute more to the standard errors. Let us denote the matrix that contains these weights as \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{\text{HC3}}\):
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{\text{HC3}} = \begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\hat{e}_1^2}{(1-h_{11})^2} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\[8pt]
0 & \dfrac{\hat{e}_2^2}{(1-h_{22})^2} & \cdots & 0 \\[8pt]
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\[8pt]
0 & 0 & \cdots & \dfrac{\hat{e}_n^2}{(1-h_{nn})^2}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
where \(h_{ii}\) are the so-called hat values (leverage) of each observation.

Hat-Values
The hat values \(h_{ii}\) are the diagonal entries of the “hat matrix” \[\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\]
This is the matrix that transforms our observed values into fitted values: \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}\). Each diagonal entry \(h_{ii}\) tells us: if we changed the observed value \(y_i\) by a small amount, how much would the fitted value \(\hat{y}_i\) change? Put more technically, \(h_{ii} = \partial \hat{y}_i / \partial y_i\).
An observation’s \(h_{ii}\) depends on how far its \(x\)-value is from the sample mean. In simple regression, we can write this as:
\[h_{ii} = \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n (x_j - \bar{x})^2}\]
An observation near the mean of \(x\) has little leverage – little pull on the regression line – so \(h_{ii}\) is close to its minimum of \(1/n\). An observation with an extreme \(x\)-value, meanwhile, has a lot of leverage: the regression line is more sensitive to its \(y\)-value, and \(h_{ii}\) is correspondingly larger, up to a maximum of 1. A value of \(h_{ii} = 1\) would mean \(\hat{y}_i = y_i\). Here, the line passes exactly through that point regardless of the other data.






Figure 1: Observations further from \(\bar{x}\) have larger hat values \(h_{ii}\), indicating greater leverage



The hat values across all observations sum to \(p\), the number of slope coefficients plus the intercept. This means there is a fixed “influence budget” shared among observations: if one observation has high leverage, the others must have less.
The HC3 correction exploits this: it divides each squared residual by \((1 - h_{ii})^2\), which inflates the contribution of high-leverage observations. The intuition is that if an influential observation also has a large residual, we should be less confident in our estimates — and the classical standard errors, which ignore this, are too optimistic.

For our model, we can calculate the values on the diagonal of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{\text{HC3}}\) as follows:

e <- resid(model2)
h <- hatvalues(model2)
omega_diag <- e^2 / (1 - h)^2
omega_diag

         1          2          3          4          5 
13.6056721  1.5638250  0.3608183 15.2726737  0.4125541 


If homoscedasticity held, the omega_diag values would all be roughly similar in magnitude — none would be dramatically larger or smaller than the rest. In such a case, a single \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) adequately describes the variability across all observations, and replacing it would be unnecessary. Figure 2 shows this scenario:






Figure 2: Simulated HC3 Weights under Homoscedasticity



As the problem of heteroscedasticity starts to increase, however, the variation of omega_diag values around \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) increases, and thus this single value can no longer summarise this variation adequately. To illustrate how much model2 suffers from heteroscedasticity, let us produce a plot like Figure 2 for it. We start by extracting \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) from model2:

sigma2 <- summary(model2)$sigma^2
sigma2

[1] 2.814863


This allows us to plot the values of omega_diag against income and to compare them to \(\hat{\sigma}^2\), shown as the orange line:

ggplot(data.frame(income = london_heterosc$income, weight = omega_diag),
       aes(x = income, y = weight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sigma2, colour = "#e57726", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = max(london_heterosc$income), y = sigma2,
           label = paste0("hat(sigma)^2 == ", round(sigma2, 2)),
           parse = TRUE, vjust = -0.8, hjust = 1, colour = "#e57726") +
  labs(x = "Income", y = "HC3 weight",
       title = expression("Diagonal entries of the HC3 " * hat(Omega) * " matrix")) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3: Diagonal entries of the HC3 \(\hat{\Omega}\) Matrix



The observation-level weights are not constant across observations as assumed by the Classical Linear Model. Some observations have weights much larger than \(\hat{\sigma}^2\), while others are much smaller. By assuming a single value \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) for all observations (the orange line), the classical model masks the large amount of variation and thus uncertainty that exists in our data. This produces standard errors that are too small — and therefore confidence intervals that are too narrow and \(p\)-values that are too optimistic.
Now conduct a significance test with robust standard errors (with the sandwich function coeftest):

coeftest(model2, vcov = vcovHC(model2, type="HC3"))

If y could also cause x, then we deal with reverse causality. | |Robust standard errors |Also known as Huber-White standard errors, correct for heteroscedasticity by adjusting the model-based standard errors using the empirical variability of the model residuals | |Sample Regression Function |A regression line based on a randomly drawn sample | |Scalar |A scalar is a single numerical value used to represent magnitude. In linear algebra, it is typically written in lowercase italic (e.g. \(a\), \(x\)). | |Secant |A straight line that intersects a curve at two or more points. The slope of a secant line gives the average rate of change between those points. | |Simultaneity |Simultaneity (or bidirectional causation) occurs when \(x\) and \(y\) influence each other at the same time, so that both \(x \rightarrow y\) and \(y \rightarrow x\) hold and neither variable is purely exogenous. | |Slope |A slope is defined as rise over run, and so it tells us how many units of y we need to climb (or descend if the slope is negative) for every additional unit of the independent variable \(x\) | |Spurious |A relationship between two variables, \(x_1\) and \(y\), is said to be spurious when it appears to exist in a simple analysis but disappears or weakens substantially once a third variable, \(x_2\), is introduced into the analysis. This suggests that the observed association between \(x_1\) and \(y\) was not causal, but rather the result of a confounding influence from \(x_2\) | |Suppressor |A suppressor variable is a variable, \(x_2\), that increases the predictive validity of another variable, \(x_1\), on an outcome \(y\) by accounting for irrelevant or misleading variance in \(x_1\). In other words, the relationship between \(x_1\) and \(y\) becomes stronger or more apparent when \(x_2\) is included in the analysis, even though \(x_2\) may have little or no direct relationship with \(y\) | |Symmetry |In the context of causation, symmetry is understood as the law-like regularity of events. There needs to be a recipe (causal mechanism) which regularly produces effects from causes | |Tangent |A straight line that touches a curve at exactly one point and has the same direction as the curve at that point. The slope of the tangent line gives the instantaneous rate of change at that point. The tangent line is the limit of secant lines as the two points get infinitely close together. | |Time-series data |Time-series data review a certain characteristic over time \(t\), where \(t\) runs from 1 to \(T\) | |Total Sum of Squares |The total variation in the dependent variable \(y\) around its mean \(\bar{y}\). It is written as: \[\text{TSS}= \sum (y_{i} - \bar{y})^{2}\] | |Variance Inflation Factor |A measure to quantify the how much larger the observed variance of a coefficient is compared to a scenario in which the variable was totally functionally independent from the other independent variables in the model | |Variance-Covariance Matrix |A variance-covariance matrix is a square matrix that encapsulates the variances of different variables on its diagonal and the covariances between pairs of variables in its off-diagonal elements. | |Vector |A vector is a list of numbers arranged in a specific order, often as a column. It represents both magnitude and direction. In notation, vectors are written in lowercase bold (e.g. \(\pmb{x}\)). Vectors are used to describe quantities like position, velocity, or coefficients in a regression model. |

title: Exam - FAQs
text:
Before the Exam
You can download these FAQs in PDF format.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: When will my examinations be taking place?
text:
When will my examinations be taking place?

For a full list of examination dates and times, please visit the Examination Dates and Times webpage.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Where will the exams take place?
text:
Where will the exams take place?

The venue information will be available in your personalised timetable. Please note that all exams will take place on the main campus. A full list of venues used for each exam session can be viewed on the Campus Maps and Exam Venues webpage. Remember that large modules may have multiple venues so please ensure you go to the venue indicated on your personalised timetable. Please note, exam venues will only appear on this page once the exam timetable for the relevant exam period has been published.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: How will I know where to sit?
text:
How will I know where to sit?

You can find your seat number in your personalised exam timetable. If you forget your seat number, there will be somebody in the exam hall with a seating plan.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I want to defer my exams. What should I do?
text:
I want to defer my exams. What should I do?

Where a student has acute personal circumstances that severely impact on their ability to sit or prepare for a complete examination period and that are evidenced, a deferral of the examination period to the next available opportunity can be requested. Students wishing to defer should speak with the PAIS Wellbeing and Academic Support Team about deferral at the first possible opportunity, but no later than five working days before the examination period starts. Find out more on how to submit a Deferral of an Examinations Period request.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I require reasonable adjustments, whom should I contact to arrange this?
text:
I require reasonable adjustments, whom should I contact to arrange this?

To be considered for reasonable adjustments, we encourage you to meet with a Disability Adviser. The Disability team’s recommendations are informed by information about your disability, including any relevant, recent medical or other professional evidence. If you do not already have any information or evidence, you can get a medical professional to complete the medical evidence form.
If you do not have any documentation related to your disability or long-term health condition, we would still encourage you to make an appointment to speak with a Disability Adviser, as there may be other options available to you.
Please note that reasonable adjustments are anticipatory and need to be made well in advance of the exam period, so please contact the Disability team as early as possible. You can find information about the relevant deadlines here.
Once your reasonable adjustments are in place, please contact the PAIS Wellbeing and Academic Support Team if you wish to discuss specific arrangements for an exam.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: How do I find out about my reasonable adjustment arrangements for my exam?
text:
How do I find out about my reasonable adjustment arrangements for my exam?

The Course Support Team will email you before your exam takes place. We aim to provide you with details of your arrangements about a week before your exam is due. Please make sure you check your university emails regularly.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I have adjustments in the exam so I can use ear plugs/anxiety aid/tablets, etc., should I let the invigilator know before the exam takes place?
text:
I have adjustments in the exam so I can use ear plugs/anxiety aid/tablets, etc., should I let the invigilator know before the exam takes place?

On the day of your exam, the invigilator should have a list provided to them about students who have reasonable adjustments and what they are. This information would have been agreed by the Disability team in advance and will be listed on each student’s personal stop-the-clock form which the invigilator will have.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: What happens if an exam starts late?
text:
What happens if an exam starts late?

While the intention is to start morning exams at 09:30 and afternoon exams at 14:00, things may happen which means the exam will start late. Please wait outside until you are called into the exam room and take your seat quickly, so that the exam can start as soon as possible. If the exam starts late, you will still be given the full time as indicated by your exam paper.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I can bring a calculator to the exam. How do I know which one I can bring?
text:
I can bring a calculator to the exam. How do I know which one I can bring?

If a calculator is permitted, you should use a battery-operated, non-programmable pocket calculator, a ‘scientific’ type which has logarithms (both common and natural), square root, etc.
Programmable calculators are not permitted.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Do I need to bring my Student ID card?
text:
Do I need to bring my Student ID card?

Yes, you must bring in your student card. During the examination, the invigilation team will be checking the picture on your ID card. If you have forgotten to bring your student ID card, a photographic ID (e.g. driving license) may be accepted in its place.
If you have no identification, you will be required to speak to an invigilator at the end of the examination and be granted the opportunity to return with your ID, only if this is located within the exam venue (e.g., in a bag/coat outside the exam room).
Students who are still unable to provide ID will be permitted to complete the examination, but their home department will be notified.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I am running late for my examination. What should I do?
text:
I am running late for my examination. What should I do?

Please give yourself enough time to arrive at the exam venue 20 minutes before your exam starts. You will not be permitted to enter the exam room 30 minutes after the exam starts. If you are late for reasons beyond your control and not permitted to take the examination, then please contact the PAIS Course Support Team without undue delay. If you are late and permitted into the examination hall, you will not be awarded extra time due to your late arrival.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: What writing equipment should I bring with me into the exam hall?
text:
What writing equipment should I bring with me into the exam hall?

Along with a calculator if permitted (see above), we advise you to bring a pen with black or blue ink, ruler, eraser. Please do not write with a red or green pen, as this will make marking your script difficult. If drawing graphs and diagrams, you may also use a pencil for drawing, but if you do so it might be advisable to go over this in pen when you are happy the diagram is correct. For answering MCQs you might want to use a pencil until you are confident of your answers.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Am I allowed to bring any smart devices or phones into the examination room?
text:
Am I allowed to bring any smart devices or phones into the examination room?

If you bring in any devices, these must be switched off, placed into the provided transparent bag, and placed under your chair. Please be aware that the standard penalty for not adhering to the above regulation is a mark of zero for the examination. Please see Regulation 10.2(6)[a] for further information.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Are bags allowed into the examination room?
text:
Are bags allowed into the examination room?

No, you are not allowed to bring any bags into the examination room. In some exam venues, there may be some baggage storage. Please note all personal property is left at your own risk.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Am I allowed to bring food into the examination room?
text:
Am I allowed to bring food into the examination room?

Food is not allowed into the examination room unless you have properly documented medical requirements. Any related documentation must be brought to the exam room and pre-approved by the PAIS Wellbeing and Academic Support Team as part of your reasonable adjustments.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: How do I identify my exam paper?
text:
How do I identify my exam paper?

You will find your exam question paper on your desk, identifiable by module title and code.

title: Exam - FAQs
text:
What is an attendance slip?

You will find an attendance slip (like the one below) on each desk. Please complete this before the exam starts. Invigilators will collect attendance slips from desks shortly after the exam begins.





By signing the attendance slip you are confirming that you do not have any form of electronic communication device on your person. If you are then found with any such item, you will be given a mark of zero.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Where do I write the answers to the questions?
text:
Where do I write the answers to the questions?

Only write your answers in the answer booklets provided. Do not write on the question paper.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Do PAIS exams have their own answer booklets?
text:
Do PAIS exams have their own answer booklets?

All POQ-coded modules with an in-person exam have specific answer booklets, and you must answer all exam questions in the provided booklet. Where there is a choice of sections to answer, you must indicate on the front cover which section is answered. You must indicate your Seat Number and Student ID on the exam booklet.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: If I need more paper to write my answers, what do I do?
text:
If I need more paper to write my answers, what do I do?

If you need more paper, raise your hand and ask for more paper from the invigilator, who will bring you 1-2 additional sheets. The additional sheets will be stapled to the relevant booklet. Please write your student ID number in the space available at the top of each additional sheet.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: What to do if I feel unwell in the exam hall?
text:
What to do if I feel unwell in the exam hall?

If you feel unwell in the exam hall, put up your hand and talk to the invigilator. In the first instance you may just be taken outside the hall to see if a small break will help. If you are not starting to feel better and need medical attendance, then the invigilator will contact relevant colleagues.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: If I need to go to the toilet during the exam, what can I do?
text:
If I need to go to the toilet during the exam, what can I do?

Raise your hand until an invigilator comes to your desk and escorts you to the toilet. You may be taking your exam in a room with 200-300 people, so please bear in mind there may be a delay as we can only take one person at a time. We will be keeping a log of everyone that is escorted to the toilet.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: If I think there is an error in the question, what do I do?
text:
If I think there is an error in the question, what do I do?

Raise your hand to speak to an invigilator who may or may not be involved in the teaching team of your module. They will convey your question to the teaching team and get back to you. This may take a while so keep working on your exam, so you do not waste time waiting for an answer. It is very likely the invigilator will return and say there is no error and ask you to proceed with your interpretation of the question. If there is indeed an error, there will be an announcement made to all students. If you have already answered the question when the announcement of any error is indicated, do not go back and redo the question, rather note on the answer booklet alongside the relevant question that you completed the question prior to the announcement.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: What happens if I write something in my examination booklet that I do not wish to be marked?
text:
What happens if I write something in my examination booklet that I do not wish to be marked?

Please cross out anything you do not want to be marked with a simple line. Make it clear to the markers that you do not wish for this to be marked.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: If I finish early, can I hand in my exam and leave the exam room?
text:
If I finish early, can I hand in my exam and leave the exam room?

Raise your hand to inform your invigilator you have finished your exam and want to hand in your script. If you are allowed to leave the room, you must do so in silence. You will not be allowed to leave the exam room within the last 20 minutes of the exam duration. Once you have left, you will not be allowed to come back into the exam room.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: Once the exam time is over, can I just get up and leave the room?
text:
Once the exam time is over, can I just get up and leave the room?

No. You will only be allowed to leave the room after the invigilators have collected all exam scripts from all desks. You will likely take your exam in a room with 200-300 people, so please be patient until all exam papers have been collected. Only then will you be allowed to leave the room in silence as other students may still be sitting their exams for other modules.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I have experienced mitigating circumstances during my examination. What should I do?
text:
I have experienced mitigating circumstances during my examination. What should I do?

If your mitigating circumstances are health (including mental health) related, please get in touch with your GP and the PAIS Wellbeing and Academic Support Team straight after the exam. It is very important that you submit documentary evidence for any mitigating circumstances affecting your performance via the personal circumstances tab on Tabula. All mitigating evidence related to in-person exams should be submitted no later than five working days following the affected exam.
Mitigation cases without proper evidence, provided in a timely manner, will not be considered by the Exam Board. Further information can be found in the Wellbeing and Support Section of the PAIS UG Handbook.

title: Exam - FAQs
section: I have accidentally left personal items in the exam room. What should I do?
text:
I have accidentally left personal items in the exam room. What should I do?

Anything left will be taken to the Examination Team, in Room JX0.15 in the Junction Building (Ground Floor). For their latest opening times, please visit the Contact Us section of their website.
